parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 60 questions. You must answer all of them. Each question carries 1.30 points. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the Scantron answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Completion and Short Answer Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains twelve completion and short answer questions. You must answer all of them. This part carries twenty two points. Write your answers on the separate answer sheet provided.

questions.stem: The molecules, which are the units of inheritance in organisms, are called
explanation_steps: A gene is a segment of DNA that carries the information for one trait; genes are passed from parents to offspring, so they are the units of inheritance (textbook G12 Unit 1 – nucleic acids carry the genetic code).
Proteins and amino acids are products of gene expression; minerals and vitamins are nutrients. Answer: B.
tips: Gene = DNA segment = unit of heredity; chromosome = long DNA molecule carrying many genes.

similar_questions.stem: The chemical substance of which genes are made is
explanation_steps: Genes are segments of DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1 The nucleic acids; 1.3.1 Mendel's work – genetic vocabulary

questions.stem: A prokaryotic cell lacks
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.17): 'A prokaryotic cell lacks a true nucleus. The DNA of a prokaryotic cell is coiled into a nucleoid region that is not surrounded by a membrane.'
Prokaryotes do have DNA, RNA and (small, 70S) ribosomes – ribosomes are not membrane-bound organelles. So E (B and C) is wrong. Answer: B.
tips: Prokaryotes lack the nucleus and MEMBRANE-BOUND organelles, but still have ribosomes.

similar_questions.stem: Which structure is found in BOTH prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
explanation_steps: Ribosomes (protein synthesis) occur in all cells. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The branch of biology that deals with the study of the classification of organisms is referred to as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.3, table of branches of biology): 'Taxonomy – the study of classification of organisms'.
Botany = plants; cytology = cells; physiology = functions of body parts; evolution = change of species over time. Answer: C.
tips: Taxis = arrangement, nomos = law: taxonomy arranges organisms into groups.

similar_questions.stem: The branch of biology that studies micro-organisms is
explanation_steps: Microbiology = study of micro-organisms. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about the function of the objective lens? It

options.C: controls the image passing through the specimen.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.7, table of microscope parts): 'Objective lens – brings image into focus and magnifies it'; 'Ocular lens (eyepiece) – magnifies the image'; 'Light source/mirror – illuminates the specimen'; the stage and clips hold the slide; the diaphragm controls the light passing on the specimen.
The function that the textbook gives only to the objective lens is bringing the image into focus. Answer: B.
The same table also says the objective magnifies, so A is also true – both are accepted.
tips: Eyepiece = magnifies; objective = focuses AND magnifies; diaphragm = amount of light; mirror/lamp = illumination.

similar_questions.stem: Which part of the light microscope controls the amount of light passing on the specimen?
explanation_steps: The diaphragm (iris) regulates the light. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two defensible options: the textbook table says the objective lens 'brings image into focus and magnifies it', so both B (keyed – the function unique to the objective in the table) and A are true. Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms is an autotroph?
explanation_steps: An autotroph makes its own organic food from simple inorganic substances (G9 p.61), usually by photosynthesis.
Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes; gymnosperms are green seed plants; algae, including the filamentous green alga Spirogyra, photosynthesise. All are autotrophs. Answer: E.
tips: Green (chlorophyll) = autotroph; fungi and animals = heterotrophs.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a heterotroph?
explanation_steps: A mushroom (fungus) has no chlorophyll and absorbs food from dead matter. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a classification at a kingdom level?
explanation_steps: The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
Chordata is a PHYLUM of the animal kingdom (animals with a notochord/backbone – G9 p.55). Answer: C.
tips: Five kingdoms: 'My Pet Fish Prefers Algae' – Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.

similar_questions.stem: Fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals are ranked as ______ of the phylum Chordata.
explanation_steps: The textbook lists them as classes of phylum Chordata. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1 The importance of classification – levels; 2.3 The five-kingdom classification

questions.stem: The valves that allow blood to flow from the atria into the ventricles, but also prevent blood from flowing back into the atria, are called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.51): 'On each of the atrioventricular canals, there are atrioventricular valves … These valves allow blood to flow from the atria into the ventricles, but prevent blood from flowing back into the atria.'
The tricuspid (right) and mitral/bicuspid (left) valves are the two individual atrioventricular valves, so the general name covering both is 'atrioventricular valves'. Answer: B.
tips: AV valves: tricuspid on the Right ('Try before you Buy': tricuspid right, bicuspid left).

similar_questions.stem: The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle has two cusps and is called the
explanation_steps: Two cusps = bicuspid = mitral valve. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An organ that is not involved in the lymphatic system is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.85): the lymphatic system 'consists of different organs, including lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, tonsils, spleen and thymus gland. These organs contain lymphatic tissue, which consists primarily of lymphocytes, but it also includes macrophages …'. Lymphocytes 'originate from red bone marrow'.
A macrophage is a CELL (a large phagocytic white blood cell), not an organ, so it cannot be 'an organ of the lymphatic system'. Answer: E.

Bone marrow is not in the textbook's list of lymphatic organs, although it produces the lymphocytes (in wider biology it is a primary lymphoid organ). D is therefore also defensible from the textbook list.
tips: Lymphatic organs: lymph nodes, tonsils, spleen, thymus (+ bone marrow as the source of lymphocytes). Macrophage = cell.

similar_questions.stem: Which lymphatic organ is found in the chest and is important for the maturation of lymphocytes in children?
explanation_steps: The thymus lies in the chest behind the sternum. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Two defensible options: E (macrophage is a cell, not an organ – keyed) and D (bone marrow is not in the textbook's list of lymphatic organs on G10 p.85, though lymphocytes originate there). Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Filamentous fungi are grouped as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.77): 'Zygomycota – The typical members of this group are filamentous and grow in cottony masses; filaments lack cross walls between adjacent cells' (e.g. black bread mould, Rhizopus).
Ascomycota = sac fungi (and yeasts); Basidiomycota = club fungi (mushrooms, rusts); Deuteromycota = imperfect fungi; lichens are fungus–alga associations, not a phylum. Answer: A.
tips: Zygo = cottony filaments (bread mould); Asco = sac; Basidio = club (mushroom); Deutero = imperfect.

similar_questions.stem: Yeasts, which are used in bread making, belong to
explanation_steps: The textbook places yeasts among the simplest ascomycota. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are adaptation mechanisms of plants to low temperature, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.142–143), low temperatures: deciduous trees shed their leaves; 'the low temperature limits soil water uptake'; conifers have needle-like leaves and thick cuticles; many plants remain dormant (rhizomes, bulbs, seeds).
Shiny leaves that reflect incident light and prevent overheating are listed under adaptations to HIGH temperatures. Answer: C.
tips: Cold: shed leaves, thick cuticle, dormancy. Heat: shiny/thin leaves, spines, sunken stomata.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an adaptation of plants to HIGH temperatures?
explanation_steps: Reflecting light prevents overheating. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment

questions.stem: Liver has all of the following functions, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.57): 'The liver removes old (non-functioning) red blood cells, excess glucose and amino acids … from the blood'; G10 p.69/131: haemoglobin of old red cells is converted to bile, which the liver secretes into the small intestine.
All four listed functions belong to the liver. Answer: E.
tips: Liver: bile, glycogen store, deamination (urea), breakdown of old red cells, detoxification.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the liver?

options.E: Breakdown of old red blood cells

explanation_steps: Insulin is made by the islets of the pancreas. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The pregnancy period is known as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.42): 'Pregnancy in humans usually lasts 38 to 40 weeks. This period of pregnancy is known as the gestation period.'
Fertilization/conception = union of sperm and ovum; contraception = preventing pregnancy; parturition = child birth. Answer: C.
tips: Gestation = time in the womb; parturition = birth.

similar_questions.stem: The process of giving birth is called
explanation_steps: Parturition (labour) ends the gestation period. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Voluntary muscles function in
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.76): 'In general, the functions of the voluntary muscles in the body include movement, facial expression, posture and respiratory movement.'
Breathing uses the skeletal (voluntary) diaphragm and intercostal muscles. All four options are correct. Answer: E.
tips: Voluntary = skeletal = striated muscle.

similar_questions.stem: Which type of muscle is found in the walls of the stomach and intestine?
explanation_steps: Smooth (involuntary) muscle produces peristalsis. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Lipids are made up of the following atoms, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.10): 'Like carbohydrates, lipids are composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. However, the number of oxygen atoms is fewer in lipids than in carbohydrates.'
Nitrogen is characteristic of proteins and nucleic acids. Answer: C.
tips: C, H, O → carbohydrates and lipids; + N → proteins; + N and P → nucleic acids.

similar_questions.stem: Which element is present in proteins but NOT in simple carbohydrates?
explanation_steps: Amino groups (–NH₂) contain nitrogen. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The process of inhaling oxygen and exhaling carbon dioxide is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.108): 'External respiration (breathing) is the process of inhaling (breathing in oxygen) and exhaling (breathing out carbon dioxide) which occurs in the lungs.'
Internal or cellular respiration is the oxidation of glucose inside the cells. Answer: D.
tips: External = lungs (breathing); internal = cells (energy release).

similar_questions.stem: The oxidation of glucose inside body cells to release energy is called
explanation_steps: It occurs within the cells. Answer: C.

questions.stem: During cellular respiration all of the following can be used as fuel, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.118): 'Though carbohydrates, fats and proteins can be used as fuel during cellular respiration, glucose is most commonly used by cells to produce energy.'
Lactic acid is a PRODUCT of anaerobic respiration (fermentation) in muscles, not one of the listed fuels. Answer: E.
tips: Fuels: carbohydrates (glucose) → fats → proteins. Lactic acid = waste product of anaerobic respiration.

similar_questions.stem: Which substance is the most commonly used respiratory fuel in cells?
explanation_steps: Glucose is most commonly used. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following human glands are classified as exocrine glands?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.1): 'The exocrine glands (sweat glands, salivary glands, tear glands, etc.) secrete juices onto a surface or into a cavity through ducts.'
The adrenal glands are ductless endocrine glands that release hormones into the blood. Answer: E (A, B and C).
tips: Exocrine = duct; endocrine = ductless, secretes hormones into blood.

similar_questions.stem: Which gland is BOTH exocrine and endocrine?
explanation_steps: The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice through a duct and insulin/glucagon into blood. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: Unit 1 introduction and summary – exocrine and endocrine glands

questions.stem: Which of the following systems do not involve the muscular system for its function?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.74): 'The muscular system helps in the proper functioning of the circulatory, digestive and respiratory systems.' G10 p.95: lymph flows because of 'the contraction of skeletal muscles, action of breathing muscles and contraction of smooth muscles in the walls of the larger lymphatic trunks'.
The nervous system CONTROLS muscles but does not depend on muscle action to carry out its own function (conducting impulses). Answer: B.
tips: Heart (cardiac muscle), peristalsis (smooth), breathing (diaphragm), lymph flow (skeletal squeezing) all need muscles.

similar_questions.stem: What moves lymph through the lymphatic vessels, since there is no pump?

options.B: Contraction of skeletal muscles and breathing movements

explanation_steps: G10 p.95 lists skeletal muscle contraction, breathing and smooth muscle of the trunks. Answer: B.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 3.2 Comparison between the lymphatic system and the circulatory system

questions.stem: A type of sugar that is commonly used in foods and drinks is
explanation_steps: Sucrose (cane or beet sugar, table sugar) is the disaccharide added to foods, tea and soft drinks; it is digested by sucrase into glucose and fructose (G10 p.38).
Maltose = malt sugar; lactose = milk sugar; starch and cellulose are polysaccharides, not table sugars. Answer: C.
tips: Table sugar = sucrose = glucose + fructose.

similar_questions.stem: The sugar found naturally in milk is
explanation_steps: Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Where do sperms mature and get stored in males?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.29): 'The epididymis is a structure formed by the union of seminiferous tubules … The epididymis is the structure in which sperms mature and are stored.'
Sperms are PRODUCED in the seminiferous tubules; the vas deferens carries them; seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids to semen. Answer: A.
tips: Made in seminiferous tubules → matured and stored in epididymis → carried by vas deferens.

similar_questions.stem: Sperm cells are produced in the
explanation_steps: Spermatogenesis takes place in the seminiferous tubules. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option E is printed 'Vas difference' in the paper (a misspelling of 'vas deferens'); paper wording kept. It does not affect the answer.

questions.stem: In a water cycle, the step that is responsible for cloud formation is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.97–98): water vapour rising into the cooler atmosphere turns back into tiny droplets 'through the process known as condensation, forming clouds'.
Evaporation and transpiration put water vapour INTO the air; precipitation is rain/snow falling from clouds. Answer: D.
tips: Vapour → droplets (condensation) = clouds.

similar_questions.stem: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of plants into the atmosphere is
explanation_steps: Transpiration returns water from plants to the air. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The tough inelastic bands (cords) that attach muscles to bones are
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.54): 'Tendons are tough inelastic bands (cords) that attach muscles to bones.'
Ligaments attach bone to bone at joints (and can stretch slightly); cartilage covers bone ends. Answer: C.
tips: Tendon: muscle→bone; ligament: bone→bone.

similar_questions.stem: The connective tissue that holds one bone to another at a joint is
explanation_steps: Ligaments bind bones together (G11 p.57). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements define the term population?

options.A: All living things in the same area that interact with one another.
options.B: Groups of organisms of the same species inhabiting the same area.
options.C: All living organisms interacting with non-living environment.
options.D: The biological role played by a species in its environment.
options.E: A place where individuals of a species live.

explanation_steps: A population is a group of individuals of the SAME species living in the same area at the same time.
Textbook (G12 p.87): 'The place where a population or an individual of a given species lives is called a habitat. The biological role played by a species in its environment is called a niche.'
A = community; C = ecosystem; D = niche; E = habitat. Answer: B.
tips: Population (one species) ⊂ community (all species) ⊂ ecosystem (+ non-living).

similar_questions.stem: All the populations of different species living and interacting in one area form a/an
explanation_steps: A community is all interacting populations in an area. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1 What is ecology? – levels of organisation, habitat, niche

questions.stem: Seedless nonvascular plants are known as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.82): 'Bryophytes include mosses and liverworts … Bryophytes lack the specialized vascular cells for conducting nutrients and water.' They reproduce by spores (no seeds).
Pteridophytes (ferns) are seedless but vascular (G9 p.83); gymnosperms, angiosperms and monocots have seeds. Answer: B.
tips: No vessels + no seeds = bryophytes; vessels + no seeds = pteridophytes.

similar_questions.stem: Ferns are classified as
explanation_steps: Ferns (pteridophytes) have vascular tissue but no seeds. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following statements indicate the functions of homeostasis, except

options.C: regulation of salt and ion content in the blood.
options.D: control of the automatic nervous system and the endocrine system.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.82–83): the skin's homeostatic functions include 'the regulation of body temperature, sensory reception and water balance'; the kidneys regulate 'salt and ion content in the blood'; the brain helps in 'controlling the autonomic nervous system and the endocrine system'.
Flexible body movement is a function of the skeletal and muscular systems (joints), not of homeostasis. Answer: E.
tips: Homeostasis organs: skin, kidneys, liver, brain.

similar_questions.stem: Which organ regulates the water level and the salt and ion content of the blood?
explanation_steps: The kidneys control water and salt balance. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option D says 'automatic nervous system'; the textbook term is 'autonomic nervous system' (paper wording kept).

questions.stem: The type of immunity that is acquired naturally when an infant receives antibodies from its mother in the first breast-milk received from an already immune mother is referred to as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.104): 'Natural acquired passive immunity: This is immunity that is acquired naturally when an unborn infant receives antibodies from its mother through the placenta or in the first breast-milk received from the already immune mother.'
Passive = ready-made antibodies received; natural = not by injection. Answer: C.
tips: Active = your body makes the antibodies; passive = you receive ready-made antibodies.

similar_questions.stem: A person receives a vaccine and later becomes immune to measles. This is
explanation_steps: Vaccines (antigens) make the body produce its own antibodies – active; given by injection – artificial. Answer: B.

questions.stem: In animals, excess glucose is stored as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.11): 'Insulin triggers the liver to convert excess glucose into glycogen.' Glycogen (animal starch) is stored in the liver and muscles (G10 p.131).
Starch is the plant storage form; insulin and glucagon are hormones. Answer: C.
tips: Plants store starch; animals store glycogen (and fat).

similar_questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates the breakdown of glycogen into glucose when blood sugar falls?
explanation_steps: Glucagon raises blood glucose. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The presence of hair in mammals is for adapting to cold temperature through
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.150): fur/feathers trap 'a layer of air next to the warm skin, improving insulation'.
Hibernation is a separate adaptation (reduced metabolism), and basking is sun-warming by reptiles; neither is performed by hair. So E (A, B and D) is wrong. Answer: B.
tips: Hair/fur/feathers + fat = insulation.

similar_questions.stem: Aquatic mammals such as whales are mainly insulated against cold by
explanation_steps: The textbook says aquatic mammals are insulated by a thick layer of fat. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.3.1 Adaptations of animals to low temperatures

questions.stem: The sexually transmitted disease syphilis is caused by
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.36): 'Syphilis is another example of an STD caused by the bacterium known as Treponema pallidum.'
Mycobacterium tuberculosis – TB; Bacillus anthracis – anthrax; Salmonella – typhoid/food poisoning; Agrobacterium – plant crown-gall. Answer: C.
tips: Syphilis = Treponema (a spiral bacterium); gonorrhoea = Neisseria.

similar_questions.stem: Tuberculosis is caused by
explanation_steps: TB is a bacterial disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.4.2 The economic importance of bacteria – syphilis

questions.review_flag: The paper spells the organism 'Treponema pallidium'; the correct name is Treponema pallidum (spelling kept in the option).

questions.stem: Xerophyte plants have all of the following adaptation mechanisms, except
explanation_steps: Xerophytes (dry-habitat plants) reduce water loss and increase uptake: thick (multi-layered) epidermis with waxy cuticle, sunken stomata, hairs around the stomata that trap moist air, and extensive root systems (G9 p.143–146).
Buoyant leaves with air spaces are an adaptation of hydrophytes (water plants). Answer: A.
tips: Xerophyte = save water; hydrophyte = float.

similar_questions.stem: Why are stomata of many xerophytes sunken in pits?

options.B: To trap humid air and reduce transpiration
options.E: To take in more water from the soil

explanation_steps: Humid air in the pit reduces the diffusion gradient for water vapour. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.unit: Unit 4 – Plants, Animals and the Environment
textbook_ref.section: 4.2.2 Adaptations of plants to water – xerophytes

questions.stem: The hormones thyroxin and calcitonin are secreted by the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.6): 'The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine and calcitonin hormones.'
Thyroxine controls the metabolic rate; calcitonin lowers blood calcium by promoting its deposition in bone (the parathyroid hormone raises it). Answer: A.
tips: Calcitonin (thyroid) lowers blood Ca²⁺; parathormone (parathyroid) raises it.

similar_questions.stem: Iodine is needed in the diet for the synthesis of
explanation_steps: Iodine is an essential component of thyroxine (G11 p.6). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The endocrine system is instrumental in regulating or coordinating all of the following body activities, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.2): 'The endocrine system is instrumental in regulating behaviour, growth, development, tissue function and metabolism, as well as sexual function and reproductive processes.'
Every option A–D is in the textbook's list, so none is an exception. Answer: E.
tips: When the stem copies a textbook list, 'None of the above' is often the key for an 'except' item.

similar_questions.stem: Compared with the nervous system, hormonal (endocrine) control is generally
explanation_steps: Hormones travel in the blood, so their effects are slower but last longer. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Answer questions 33 and 34 using the following figure, which shows a solution where an animal cell is immersed in it. The solute (salt) concentration of the solution and the cell are indicated. (Figure: an animal cell whose contents are 20% salt is immersed in a beaker of solution that is 10% salt; dots show water molecules both inside and outside the cell.) The solution where the animal cell is immersed in is a/an
questions.image_alt: A beaker of solution with dots representing water molecules scattered through it; the solution is labelled '10% Salt'. Inside the beaker is an irregular animal cell, labelled 'an animal cell', whose contents are labelled '20% Salt'. An arrow labels one dot as 'water molecule'.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.21): 'A hypotonic solution is a solution with a lower solute concentration' (compared with the cell contents); hypertonic = higher; isotonic = equal.
The surrounding solution has 10% salt while the cell contents have 20% salt, so the solution has the LOWER solute concentration – it is hypotonic to the cell. Answer: A.
tips: Always compare the OUTSIDE solution with the INSIDE of the cell.

similar_questions.stem: A red blood cell (about 0.9% salt inside) is placed in 5% salt solution. The solution is
explanation_steps: 5% > 0.9%: the outside is more concentrated – hypertonic. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3.2 The transportation of molecules – osmosis and solutions

questions.stem: Using the same figure (an animal cell with 20% salt inside is immersed in a 10% salt solution), what happens to the cell if it is left in the solution for some time?
questions.image_alt: A beaker of solution with dots representing water molecules scattered through it; the solution is labelled '10% Salt'. Inside the beaker is an irregular animal cell, labelled 'an animal cell', whose contents are labelled '20% Salt'. An arrow labels one dot as 'water molecule'.

options.A: The cell will gain water and grow larger.
options.B: Water will move into the cell.
options.C: The cell will shrink and collapse.
options.D: The cell is in danger of bursting.

explanation_steps: Water moves by osmosis from the dilute (hypotonic) solution into the more concentrated cell contents (B).
The cell therefore gains water and swells (A); an animal cell has no cell wall, so it may burst (lyse) (D).
Shrinking (C) happens only in a hypertonic solution. A, B and D are all correct. Answer: E.
tips: Hypotonic outside → animal cell swells and may burst; plant cell becomes turgid (wall prevents bursting).

similar_questions.stem: What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution?

options.C: It loses water and becomes plasmolysed

explanation_steps: Water leaves the cell; the cytoplasm shrinks away from the wall (plasmolysis). Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3.2 The transportation of molecules – osmosis in animal cells

questions.stem: Living cells were, for the first time, observed by the Dutch naturalist called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.11): 'Living cells were observed first in the mid-seventeenth century by the Dutch naturalist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. He called the tiny organisms that he observed "animalcules".'
Robert Hooke saw and named dead cork 'cells'; Schleiden and Schwann proposed the cell theory; Darwin – evolution. Answer: C.
tips: Hooke named cells (dead cork); Leeuwenhoek saw LIVING cells first.

similar_questions.stem: The scientist who first used the word 'cell' after observing thin slices of cork was
explanation_steps: Robert Hooke (1665). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The number of red blood cells generally increases due to the following conditions, except
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.69): 'The number of red blood cells generally increases following exercise, a large meal, a rise in temperature or an increase in altitude.'
All four conditions increase the count, so none is an exception. Answer: E.
tips: Textbook lists (exercise, meal, temperature, altitude) are often tested word-for-word.

similar_questions.stem: A deficiency of red blood cells or of haemoglobin is called
explanation_steps: Anaemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood (G10 p.69). Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3.2 Blood cells – red blood cell counts

questions.stem: Galapagos Islands, where Darwin conducted his study, are found in/near
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.63): after exploring the coasts of South America, 'the Beagle then sailed to the Galapagos Islands, west of Ecuador', where Darwin studied giant tortoises and finches.
Ecuador is in South America. Answer: E.
tips: Darwin's finches – Galapagos – off Ecuador, South America (voyage of HMS Beagle).

similar_questions.stem: On the Galapagos Islands, Darwin was especially struck by the variety of
explanation_steps: Each island had its own forms of finches and tortoises. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Denitrification converts

options.A: nitrogen gas into nitrate and nitrite.
options.B: nitrogen into ammonium salt and ammonia.
options.C: nitrates and nitrites into nitrogen gas.
options.E: ammonium salts into nitrous gas and nitrite.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.97): 'Denitrification is the opposite of nitrogen fixation and converts nitrates (NO₃⁻) and nitrites (NO₂⁻) in the soil into nitrogen gas or gaseous compounds, such as nitrous oxide or nitric oxide.' It is done by anaerobic bacteria such as Pseudomonas.
B = nitrogen fixation; D = nitrification. Answer: C.
tips: Fixation: N₂ → NH₃; nitrification: NH₃ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻; denitrification: NO₃⁻ → N₂.

similar_questions.stem: The conversion of ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter is called
explanation_steps: Oxidation of ammonia to nitrate = nitrification. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a function of lipids?

options.A: Lipids are important sources of energy.
options.B: Lipids are used for food storage.
options.C: They are components of a cell membrane.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.11) lists the functions of lipids: sources of energy; food storage molecules; phospholipids are the main components of the cell membrane; adipose tissue under the skin gives insulation, reducing heat loss.
Enzymes are proteins, not lipids. Answer: E.
tips: Enzymes = proteins. Lipids = energy, storage, membranes, insulation (and some hormones).

similar_questions.stem: Enzymes are biological catalysts made of
explanation_steps: Enzymes are proteins. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Magnesium deficiency causes
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.13, minerals table): Magnesium – deficiency: 'Muscle weakness (fatigue), cramps'.
Swelling of the thyroid (goitre) = iodine; headaches and anaemia = iron; reduced growth and badly formed teeth = calcium. Answer: A.
tips: Ca – bones/teeth; Fe – anaemia; I – goitre; Mg – muscle weakness, cramps.

similar_questions.stem: Goitre (swelling of the thyroid gland) is caused by a deficiency of
explanation_steps: Iodine is needed for thyroxine. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Vascular plant tissue includes all of the following cell types, except
explanation_steps: Xylem is made of vessels and tracheids (plus fibres and parenchyma); phloem of sieve tubes/sieve cells, companion cells and phloem parenchyma (G11 p.115).
Cambium cells are meristematic (dividing) cells lying BETWEEN xylem and phloem; they produce new xylem and phloem but are not themselves conducting cells (G11 p.123). Answer: E.
Caution: the textbook (G11 p.112) states 'Vascular tissue includes xylem, phloem, parenchyma and cambium cells', which would make every option part of vascular tissue.
tips: Xylem: vessels + tracheids; phloem: sieve tubes + companion cells; cambium: dividing layer between them.

similar_questions.stem: Which cells of the phloem carry out the transport of dissolved food?
explanation_steps: Sieve tubes carry dissolved food (G11 p.115). Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 6.2 Plant tissues – vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)

questions.review_flag: Textbook conflict: G11 p.112 lists cambium cells as part of vascular tissue, so strictly no option is excluded. E (cambium – meristematic, not a conducting cell) is keyed as the examiner's evident intent. 'Sieve cells' (gymnosperm phloem) is not a textbook term (the book uses sieve tubes). Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about ligaments? They

options.A: are composed of strands of collagen fibers.
options.B: are capable of being stretched slightly.
options.C: are arranged in a crisscross pattern.
options.D: control the ranges of motion of a joint.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.57): 'Ligaments are composed of strands of collagen fibres. While ligaments are capable of being stretched slightly, they are arranged in a crisscross pattern, in order to prevent the joints from becoming loose. Ligaments control the range of motion of a joint …'
All four statements are correct, so there is no incorrect one. Answer: E.
tips: Ligaments: collagen, slightly stretchy, criss-cross, limit joint movement.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE of tendons?

options.B: They are elastic and stretch a lot
options.C: They are tough inelastic cords joining muscle to bone
options.D: They cover the ends of bones

explanation_steps: G11 p.54 definition. Answer: C.

questions.stem: A dehydration reaction typically produces
explanation_steps: A dehydration (condensation) reaction joins small molecules (monomers) into a larger molecule by removing water (G10 p.3: 'Condensation is the formation of a larger molecule by releasing a water molecule').

Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in dehydration reactions to form polypeptides/proteins – a typical dehydration product. Fatty acids, amino acids and glucose are monomers, the products of HYDROLYSIS of lipids, proteins and starch. Answer: C.
tips: Dehydration synthesis builds polymers (–H₂O); hydrolysis breaks them (+H₂O).

similar_questions.stem: Hydrolysis of a disaccharide such as maltose produces
explanation_steps: Adding water breaks maltose into two glucose molecules. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Darwin's theory was criticized because he

options.A: gave satisfactory explanation for the source of variation.
options.B: described survival of the fittest but not arrival of the fittest.
options.C: did not distinguish between phenotypic and genotypic variations.
options.D: believed that favourable variations were inherited.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.64), Criticism of Darwinism: '1. He was unable to give a satisfactory explanation for the source of variation. He described the survival of the fittest, but not the arrival of the fittest. 2. He did not distinguish between phenotypic and genotypic variation. 3. He believed that favourable variation (both genotypic and phenotypic) was inherited.'
B, C and D copy the criticisms; A is the first criticism with the word 'unable' missing. The examiner clearly means all the listed criticisms. Answer: E.
tips: Darwin could not explain the SOURCE of variation (mutation and genes were discovered later – neo-Darwinism).

similar_questions.stem: Neo-Darwinism improved Darwin's theory mainly by adding

options.A: the idea of use and disuse
options.B: knowledge of genetics and mutation as sources of variation

explanation_steps: Mendel's genetics and de Vries's mutation explained variation (G12 p.64). Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option A as printed ('gave satisfactory explanation for the source of variation') is the opposite of the textbook criticism ('was unable to give a satisfactory explanation'); a word appears to be missing. E is keyed as intended; if A is read literally, B, C and D are all individually correct and there is no single best answer. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: A failure by an organism to evolve in response to environmental change can lead it to
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.61): 'Continuous evolution over many generations can result in the development of new varieties and species. Likewise, a failure to evolve in response to environmental changes can lead to extinction.' Answer: B.
tips: Adapt (evolve) or die out.

similar_questions.stem: Structures such as the human appendix that are reduced and have little or no function are called
explanation_steps: They are evidence of evolution from comparative anatomy. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Small openings on an insect's body, which are used for gaseous exchange are the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.99): 'Insects have no lungs, but possess small openings on their bodies called spiracles, which are used for gaseous exchange.' They lead into a system of tracheae.
The osculum is the large opening of a sponge; antennae are sense organs. Answer: D.
tips: Insects: spiracles → tracheae; fish: gills; sponges: osculum (water out).

similar_questions.stem: Air entering an insect's spiracles is carried to the tissues by tubes called
explanation_steps: The tracheal system delivers air directly to cells. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The nitrogen bases of nucleic acids, known as pyrimidines, are
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.3): adenine and guanine have a two-ring structure (purines); 'cytosine (C), thymine (T), and uracil (U), have a single-ring structure and are known as pyrimidines'. Answer: C.
tips: 'CUT the PYe' – C, U, T are pyrimidines; 'Pure As Gold' – purines A, G.

similar_questions.stem: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
explanation_steps: RNA has uracil in place of thymine. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Sense of smell is perceived by the
explanation_steps: Smell receptors in the nasal lining send impulses along the olfactory nerve to the brain 'through the olfactory bulb' (G10 p.144–145). The olfactory lobes (bulbs) of the forebrain are the brain region concerned with smell. Answer: C.
The textbook (G10 p.173) also says the sensory area of the CEREBRUM 'receives impulses from the sense organs and interprets them as sight, hearing, smell, taste …' – so D is defensible too.
The pituitary and hypothalamus are endocrine/control centres; the medulla controls breathing and heartbeat.
tips: Olfactory = smell (olfactory nerve → olfactory bulb/lobe → cerebral cortex).

similar_questions.stem: Which part of the brain coordinates muscular action to maintain balance?
explanation_steps: The cerebellum coordinates balance (G10 p.173). Answer: B.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 8.2.1 The central nervous system – cerebrum (sensory area)

questions.review_flag: Two defensible options: C (olfactory lobe – keyed; the textbook mentions the olfactory bulb/nerve) and D (cerebrum – the textbook says its sensory area interprets smell). Both accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Codon is the information carried by the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.5): 'The information that mRNA carries is written in genetic code. Each genetic code carries three letters of the nucleotide bases and is called a codon. Each codon on mRNA specifies one amino acid.'
tRNA carries the complementary ANTICODON; rRNA forms ribosomes. Answer: A.
tips: Codon on mRNA; anticodon on tRNA; triplet on DNA.

similar_questions.stem: If an mRNA codon is AUG, the anticodon on the tRNA is
explanation_steps: Pairing A–U, U–A, G–C gives UAC. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Alveoli, the efficient gas exchange sites in the lungs, are characterized by

options.B: tube like structures for air passage.
options.D: cilia on their surfaces for filtering dust.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.110): 'Each terminal bronchiole gives rise to a number of thin-walled, bag-like structures called alveoli … A single layer of epithelial cells lines each alveolus', surrounded by capillaries; the surfaces are moist so gases dissolve and diffuse.
Tube-like air passages with cilia are the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles, not alveoli. Answer: E (A and C).
tips: Good exchange surface: large area, thin, moist, well supplied with blood.

similar_questions.stem: Which feature does NOT help alveoli exchange gases efficiently?
explanation_steps: Cartilage rings keep the trachea and bronchi open; they are not in alveoli. Answer: D.

questions.stem: A woman with heterozygous blood type A can give birth to a child with blood type B, if the genotype of the father's blood type is
explanation_steps: Mother (heterozygous A) = IᴬIⁱ; she gives Iᴬ or Iⁱ. A blood-group-B child must be IᴮIⁱ (IᴮIᴮ is impossible because the mother has no Iᴮ), so the child needs Iⁱ from the mother and Iᴮ from the father.
IᴮIᴮ father: all children receive Iᴮ – ½ are IᴮIⁱ (group B). IᴬIᴮ father: ¼ IᴮIⁱ (group B). IᴮIⁱ father: ¼ IᴮIⁱ (group B).
IᴬIⁱ father has no Iᴮ allele, so a group-B child is impossible. Answer: E (A, B and D).
tips: For a child to show B, someone must pass Iᴮ – check which fathers carry it.

similar_questions.stem: A man of blood group AB marries a woman of blood group O. Which blood group is IMPOSSIBLE for their children?

options.C: Both A and B are possible; AB is impossible

explanation_steps: IᴬIᴮ × IⁱIⁱ → IᴬIⁱ (A) or IᴮIⁱ (B), each ½; no AB or O children. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The lymphatic system is different from the circulatory system because it

options.A: carries macrophages involved in the immune response.
options.D: removes metabolic wastes from the body.
options.E: keeps the fluid balance in the interstitial spaces.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.94): 'The function of the lymphatic system is to keep the fluid balance in the interstitial spaces. The substances that leak from the capillaries are collected and returned to the blood circulation by the lymphatic system.'

B, C and D describe the blood circulatory system (the heart pumps blood; blood carries nutrients, oxygen and wastes). Blood also carries white cells (monocytes that become macrophages), so A is not a difference. Answer: E.
tips: Lymph: one-way, no pump, returns tissue fluid; blood: two-way, pumped by the heart.

similar_questions.stem: Unlike the blood circulatory system, the lymphatic system

options.B: is a one-way system from the tissue spaces to the blood
options.D: moves in a closed double circuit

explanation_steps: G10 p.95: lymph travels in only one direction, from interstitial spaces to the blood. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.2 Comparison between the lymphatic system and the circulatory system

questions.stem: The type of plant tissues that have many chloroplasts in their cells are called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.113): parenchyma cells containing many chloroplasts form a 'type of tissue called chlorenchyma. The chief function of this type of tissue is photosynthesis.' Answer: B.
tips: Chlor- = green (chlorophyll): chlorenchyma = photosynthetic parenchyma.

similar_questions.stem: Which plant tissue has thick, lignified walls and gives strength and support?
explanation_steps: Sclerenchyma cells have thick lignified walls. Answer: C.

questions.stem: In a test cross, to get 25% homozygous recessive individuals in the F₁ generation, the parents' genotype for the trait should be

options.B: one homozygous dominant and one heterozygous.
options.E: one homozygous recessive and one heterozygous.

explanation_steps: Check each cross for the fraction aa: AA × AA → 0; AA × Aa → 0; Aa × Aa → ¼ aa (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa); aa × aa → 100% aa; Aa × aa → ½ aa.
Only two heterozygous parents give 25% homozygous recessive offspring. Answer: C.
Note: a true test cross (G12 p.37) is a cross with the homozygous recessive (option E), which gives 50%, not 25%, recessive offspring – so the phrase 'test cross' in the stem is used loosely.
tips: Aa × Aa → 3:1 phenotypes, ¼ recessive; Aa × aa (test cross) → 1:1.

similar_questions.stem: A tall pea plant crossed with a short (tt) plant gives 50% tall and 50% short offspring. The tall parent was
explanation_steps: Tt × tt → ½ Tt : ½ tt. A TT parent would give all tall. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Stem inconsistency: a test cross is by definition a cross with the homozygous recessive (option E), which gives 50% recessive offspring, while 25% requires both parents heterozygous (C). C keyed because it matches the 25% figure. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Two sister chromatids are held together at the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.16): 'They are now visible as two separate strands, called sister chromatids, held together at a point along their length called the centromere.'
Centrioles organise the spindle; chiasmata are crossing-over points between HOMOLOGOUS chromosomes in meiosis. Answer: A.
tips: Centromere joins chromatids; centriole makes spindle; chiasma = crossing over.

similar_questions.stem: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs at points called
explanation_steps: Chiasmata form in prophase I of meiosis. Answer: B.

questions.stem: When a young animal forms a strong attachment to an individual, this is called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.189): 'Imprinting is a form of learning that is limited to a specific time period in an animal's life that is generally irreversible. When a young animal forms a strong attachment to an individual, usually one of the parents …'. Answer: B.
tips: Imprinting – ducklings follow the first moving object they see (Lorenz's geese).

similar_questions.stem: A bird stops reacting to a scarecrow after seeing it many times without harm. This is
explanation_steps: Learning to ignore an irrelevant stimulus = habituation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Answer questions 57 and 58 using the following chemical equation of an anaerobic respiration that takes place in animal cells: Glucose → X + Energy (Y ATP). The amount of energy, in ATP, produced in this fermentation reaction is
explanation_steps: In anaerobic respiration only glycolysis yields ATP: glucose is split into two pyruvic acid molecules 'releasing two molecules of ATP' (G10 p.118); in animal (muscle) cells the pyruvate is then reduced to lactic acid with no further ATP.
Net gain = 2 ATP per glucose (aerobic respiration gives 36–38). Answer: B.
tips: Anaerobic = 2 ATP; aerobic = 36 (textbook) or 38 ATP.

similar_questions.stem: How many times more ATP does aerobic respiration (36 ATP) give per glucose than anaerobic respiration?
explanation_steps: 36 ÷ 2 = 18. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 5.3 Cellular respiration – glycolysis and anaerobic respiration

questions.stem: Using the same equation of anaerobic respiration in animal cells (Glucose → X + Energy (Y ATP)), the product represented by the letter "X" is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.119): lactic acid fermentation is carried out 'sometimes by the muscle cells of animals' when oxygen is short: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 lactic acid + energy.
Alcohol and carbon dioxide are the products of alcoholic fermentation in yeast and plants; water and CO₂ come from aerobic respiration. Answer: C.
tips: Animals → lactic acid (cramp); yeast → ethanol + CO₂ (bread, beer).

similar_questions.stem: The products of anaerobic respiration in yeast are
explanation_steps: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about the systole and diastole of the cardiac cycle?

options.A: Atrial systole is the contraction of the atrial muscles.
options.B: Atrial diastole is relaxation of the atrial muscles.
options.C: Ventricular diastole is the contraction of the ventricular muscles.
options.D: Ventricular systole is the contraction of the ventricular muscles.
options.E: Ventricular diastole is relaxation of the ventricular muscles.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.53): 'systole' means to contract, 'diastole' to dilate; ventricular systole is contraction of the ventricular muscles and ventricular diastole is their relaxation.
C calls ventricular diastole a contraction – incorrect. Answer: C.
tips: Systole = Squeeze; Diastole = Dilate (relax).

similar_questions.stem: During ventricular systole blood is pumped into the
explanation_steps: Contracting ventricles push blood through the semilunar valves into the arteries. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.1.1 The human heart – systole and diastole

questions.stem: All of the following plant structures are correctly matched with their function, except

options.A: sieve tube ---- transport of dissolved food.
options.B: phloem parenchyma ---- act as storage and packaging.
options.C: root cap ---- protects delicate root tips.
options.D: flower ---- production of male and female gametes.
options.E: mesophyll ---- formation of phloem and xylem.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.115): sieve tubes carry out 'the transport of dissolved food'; 'phloem parenchyma … act as storage and packaging tissue'. The root cap protects the delicate root tip; the flower produces the gametes (pollen and ovules).
The mesophyll (palisade and spongy layers) is the photosynthetic tissue of the leaf (G11 p.126–127). New xylem and phloem are formed by the CAMBIUM (G11 p.123). Answer: E.
tips: Mesophyll = photosynthesis; cambium = new xylem and phloem.

similar_questions.stem: The palisade layer of the leaf mesophyll is specialised for
explanation_steps: Its long cells contain many chloroplasts. Answer: B.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 6.4.1 The stem; 6.4.2 The leaf – cambium and mesophyll

questions.stem: Different microscopes use different sources of illumination. Write the sources of illumination of the following microscopes. 1.1 Light microscope: ____ 1.2 Electron microscope: ____ (1 point)
questions.answer: 1.1 Light microscope: (visible) light – from a mirror or a lamp (bulb). 1.2 Electron microscope: a beam of electrons.

subparts.question: Source of illumination of the light microscope
Source of illumination of the electron microscope

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.6): the light microscope 'uses light (visible light) as a source of illumination to see the specimen on the stage'.

Textbook (G9 p.7): the electron microscope 'uses a beam of electrons as a source of illumination for the specimen'; electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light, so it has a much higher magnifying and resolving power (viruses, internal cell structures).
marking_points: 1.1 light / visible light / sunlight via mirror / electric bulb (½)
1.2 beam (stream) of electrons (½)
tips: Light microscope → glass lenses; electron microscope → electromagnets focus the electron beam.

similar_questions.stem: Why can an electron microscope show a virus while a school light microscope cannot?
similar_questions.answer: Because the electron microscope uses a beam of electrons, which gives a much higher magnification and resolution than visible light.
explanation_steps: Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the illumination; electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.3 The microscope – light and electron microscopes

questions.stem: Allocate the following animals according to their body symmetry: (Cnidarians, Sponges, Platyhelminthes). 2.1 Asymmetric: ____ 2.2 Radial symmetry: ____ 2.3 Bilateral symmetry: ____ (1.5 points)
questions.answer: 2.1 Asymmetric – sponges (Porifera); 2.2 radial symmetry – cnidarians (e.g. Hydra, jellyfish); 2.3 bilateral symmetry – Platyhelminthes (flatworms).

subparts.question: Asymmetric
steps: No plane divides a sponge into similar halves.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G9 p.89): 'Sponges are the simplest of all animals. They have an asymmetric body' – they cannot be cut into similar halves.
Textbook (G9 p.90): 'Cnidarians have a simple, radially symmetrical body plan' – body parts arranged around a central axis, so any plane through the axis gives identical halves.
Textbook (G9 p.91): flatworms have 'simple bilateral symmetry and cephalization' – only one plane gives mirror-image left and right halves.
marking_points: ½ point for each correct allocation (sponges – asymmetric; cnidarians – radial; Platyhelminthes – bilateral)
tips: Sponge (none) → Cnidarian (radial, sessile/floating) → Flatworm (bilateral, head end).

similar_questions.stem: What is cephalization, and which of the three groups (sponges, cnidarians, flatworms) shows it?
similar_questions.answer: Cephalization is the development of the front (anterior) end of the body into a definite head; flatworms (Platyhelminthes) show it.
explanation_steps: G9 p.91: Platyhelminthes have a definite head at the anterior end; bilateral symmetry goes with forward movement.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3.5 Kingdom Animalia – symmetry; Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes

questions.stem: Amino acids are classified as essential or non-essential amino acids. Write the difference between essential and non-essential amino acids. 3.1 Essential amino acids: ____ 3.2 Non-essential amino acids: ____ (1 point)
questions.answer: 3.1 Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised (made) by the body, so they must be obtained from the diet. 3.2 Non-essential amino acids can be synthesised by the body (from other amino acids/nutrients), so they need not be supplied in the diet.

subparts.question: Essential amino acids
subparts.answer: Cannot be made by the body; must come from food

subparts.question: Non-essential amino acids
subparts.answer: Can be made (synthesised) by the body

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.8): 'Proteins containing essential amino acids (those that the body cannot synthesize) are called complete proteins' – e.g. casein in milk.
Non-essential amino acids are those the body can make itself, e.g. by converting other amino acids in the liver.
About 20 amino acids occur in proteins; in adults about 8–9 are essential.
marking_points: 3.1 not synthesised by the body / must be taken in the diet (½)
3.2 synthesised by the body (½)
tips: 'Essential' = essential IN THE DIET, not more important for the body.

similar_questions.stem: What is a complete protein? Give one example.
similar_questions.answer: A protein that contains all the essential amino acids, e.g. casein in milk (also egg and meat proteins).
explanation_steps: G10 p.8: proteins lacking one or more essential amino acids are incomplete.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.2 Proteins – essential and non-essential amino acids

questions.stem: Identify the following parts of the ear: 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5. (2.5 points) (Figure: section of the human ear with brackets for the outer, middle and inner ear. 4.1 – the membrane at the inner end of the ear canal, at the boundary with the middle ear; 4.2 – three looped canals at the top of the inner ear; 4.3 – the snail-shaped coiled tube of the inner ear; 4.4 – the tube running from the middle ear down towards the throat; 4.5 – the tube leading inward from the opening of the outer ear.)
questions.image_alt: Cross-section of the human ear (the same drawing as textbook G10 Figure 7.9) with brackets for outer ear, middle ear and inner ear. 4.1: pointer from the middle-ear bracket to the thin membrane at the inner end of the ear canal. 4.2: two pointers to the three looped canals at the top of the inner ear. 4.3: pointer to the snail-shaped coiled tube of the inner ear. 4.4: pointer to the tube running downwards and forwards from the middle ear towards the throat. 4.5: pointer to the tube leading from the outer ear opening inwards.
questions.answer: 4.1 Eardrum (tympanic membrane / tympanum); 4.2 semicircular canals; 4.3 cochlea; 4.4 Eustachian tube; 4.5 auditory canal (ear canal, external auditory meatus).

subparts.question: Part 4.1
steps: Boundary between outer and middle ear.

explanation_steps: The drawing is the textbook's Figure 7.9 (G10 p.155), whose labels are eardrum, semicircular canals, cochlea, Eustachian tube and auditory canal.
4.1: 'The auditory canal ends in the eardrum. This thin membrane separates the external ear from the middle ear' (G10 p.155).
4.2: semicircular canals – three canals at right angles, for balance (G10 p.156).
4.3: cochlea – snail-shaped front part of the inner ear, for hearing (G10 p.156).
4.4: 'The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to pharynx' and equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum (G10 p.156).
4.5: auditory canal – carries sound from the pinna to the eardrum; lined with hairs and wax glands (G10 p.155).
marking_points: ½ point each: eardrum/tympanum; semicircular canals; cochlea; Eustachian tube; auditory canal/external auditory meatus
4.1: 'ossicles/hammer' may be accepted at the teacher's discretion only if the scan pointer is read as ending on the malleus
tips: Outer ear: pinna, auditory canal, eardrum. Middle ear: ossicles, Eustachian tube. Inner ear: cochlea (hearing), semicircular canals (balance).

similar_questions.stem: Name the three ossicles of the middle ear in order from the eardrum, and state their function.
similar_questions.answer: Malleus (hammer) → incus (anvil) → stapes (stirrup); they transmit and amplify the vibrations of the eardrum to the oval window of the inner ear.
explanation_steps: G10 p.156: the malleus is attached to the eardrum; the incus links the malleus to the stapes.

questions.stem: In the female reproductive system, the process by which the ovum matures is called 5.1 ____. If it is not fertilized, 5.2 ____ cycle follows, and the time this cycle ceases because of age is called 5.3 ____. (1.5 points)

subparts.question: Cycle that follows if not fertilised
End of the cycle with age

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.34): 'The production of ova in the ovaries is called oogenesis. The release of a mature ovum from the ovary is called ovulation.'
If the ovum is not fertilised, the thickened uterine lining breaks down and is shed – the menstrual cycle (about 28 days) continues.
'Menopause is the cessation of the menstrual cycle' (G11 p.34), usually at about 45–55 years of age.
marking_points: ½ point each: oogenesis; menstrual (menstruation); menopause
5.1: 'ovulation' is the release, not the maturation, of the ovum – teacher's discretion
tips: Oogenesis (making) → ovulation (release) → menstruation (no fertilisation) → menopause (stops).

similar_questions.stem: What is ovulation, and roughly on which day of a 28-day menstrual cycle does it occur?
similar_questions.answer: Ovulation is the release of a mature ovum from the ovary; it occurs at about day 14.
explanation_steps: G11 p.34 defines ovulation; mid-cycle LH surge triggers it.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3 The female reproductive system – oogenesis, menstruation, menopause

questions.review_flag: 5.1 'the process by which the ovum matures' is keyed as oogenesis (textbook: 'production of ova'); some students may write ovulation (release of the mature ovum). Teacher decision on partial credit.

questions.stem: Write the three components that make a nucleotide. 6.1 ____ 6.2 ____ 6.3 ____ (1.5 points)
questions.answer: 6.1 A five-carbon (pentose) sugar – deoxyribose in DNA or ribose in RNA; 6.2 a phosphate group; 6.3 a nitrogenous base (adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine or uracil).
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.2): 'Each nucleotide consists of three sub-units: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.'
Base + sugar alone = nucleoside; adding the phosphate makes a nucleotide.
marking_points: ½ point each: pentose (five-carbon) sugar / ribose or deoxyribose; phosphate; nitrogenous base (any order)
tips: Nucleotide = Phosphate + Sugar + Base ('PSB').

similar_questions.stem: How does the sugar in an RNA nucleotide differ from that in a DNA nucleotide?
similar_questions.answer: RNA contains ribose; DNA contains deoxyribose (which has one oxygen atom less).
explanation_steps: Both are five-carbon (pentose) sugars.

questions.stem: Match the following food processing mechanisms listed in column (A) with the terms in column (B). Column A: 7.1 Digestion, 7.2 Ingestion, 7.3 Absorption, 7.4 Assimilation, 7.5 Egestion. Column B: A. anus, B. cell, C. mouth, D. enzyme, E. intestine. (2.5 points)
questions.answer: 7.1 Digestion – D (enzyme); 7.2 Ingestion – C (mouth); 7.3 Absorption – E (intestine); 7.4 Assimilation – B (cell); 7.5 Egestion – A (anus).
explanation_steps: Ingestion = taking food into the body through the MOUTH.
Digestion = breakdown of large insoluble food into small soluble molecules, speeded up by ENZYMES (G10 p.21).
Absorption = 'the transfer of these smaller molecules into the bloodstream' through the wall of the (small) INTESTINE (G10 p.22).
Assimilation = 'nutrients are incorporated by CELLS to be used for various activities within the cells' (G10 p.22).
Egestion = elimination of undigested food; 'the elimination of solid faeces from the body through the ANUS is called defecation' (G10 p.22).
marking_points: ½ point for each correct match: 7.1 D, 7.2 C, 7.3 E, 7.4 B, 7.5 A
tips: Order of food processing: ingestion → digestion → absorption → assimilation → egestion.

similar_questions.stem: Arrange the five stages of food processing in the correct order and name where the absorption of digested food mainly takes place.
similar_questions.answer: Ingestion → digestion → absorption → assimilation → egestion; absorption mainly takes place in the small intestine (villi).
explanation_steps: Villi give the small intestine a very large surface area for absorption.

questions.stem: Write the three main plasma protein groups. 8.1 ____ 8.2 ____ 8.3 ____ (1.5 points)
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.67): 'The three main plasma protein groups are albumin, globulin, and fibrinogen.'
Albumins keep the osmotic pressure of blood; globulins include antibodies that fight disease; fibrinogen is needed for blood clotting.
marking_points: ½ point each: albumin; globulin (antibodies/gamma globulin); fibrinogen (any order)
tips: 'AGF' – Albumin (osmotic balance), Globulin (antibodies), Fibrinogen (clotting).

similar_questions.stem: Which plasma protein is converted into fibrin during blood clotting?
explanation_steps: Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap blood cells.

questions.stem: Match the endocrine glands in column A with the resulting symptoms or diseases in column B (which result when there is an abnormal hormone secretion). Column A: 9.1 Pituitary, 9.2 Thyroid, 9.3 Adrenal, 9.4 Pancreas. Column B: A. Addison's disease, B. Diabetes, C. Gigantism, D. Goiter. (2 points)
questions.answer: 9.1 Pituitary – C (gigantism); 9.2 Thyroid – D (goiter); 9.3 Adrenal – A (Addison's disease); 9.4 Pancreas – B (diabetes).
explanation_steps: Pituitary: 'An overproduction of the growth hormone during childhood results in gigantism' (G11 p.17).
Thyroid: a shortage of iodine/thyroxine makes the thyroid enlarge – goitre (G10 p.13; G11 p.17–18).
Adrenal: 'failure of the adrenal cortex causes Addison's disease' (G11 p.20).
Pancreas: 'Failure of insulin secretion causes a disease called diabetes mellitus' (G11 p.19).
marking_points: ½ point for each correct match: 9.1 C, 9.2 D, 9.3 A, 9.4 B
tips: Pituitary–growth, thyroid–goitre, adrenal–Addison's/Cushing's, pancreas–diabetes.

similar_questions.stem: What disorder results from too little growth hormone in childhood, and which gland is involved?
explanation_steps: G11 p.17: abnormal pituitary function leads to gigantism or dwarfism.

questions.stem: The following table shows the estimated number of organisms recorded in a natural ecosystem: Plants 100, Snakes 60, Ducks 10, Toads 175, Grasshopper 1500. Using the given data construct a pyramid of numbers. (2 points)
questions.answer: Arrange the organisms by feeding (trophic) level, producers at the bottom, and draw a bar for each level whose width is proportional to the number: Plants 100 (producers, base) → Grasshoppers 1500 (primary consumers) → Toads 175 (secondary consumers) → Snakes 60 (tertiary consumers) → Ducks 10 (top consumers). The grasshopper bar is the widest; the plant bar is narrower than it (a few large plants feed many insects), so the pyramid is partly inverted at the base; above the grasshoppers the bars get steadily narrower to the ducks at the apex.

answer_tables.title: Pyramid of numbers (top to bottom)
answer_tables.note: Bar lengths are only roughly to scale. The base is narrower than the level above because a few large plants (e.g. trees/bushes) support many grasshoppers – the partly inverted pyramid of textbook Figure 3.14b.

explanation_steps: Food chain implied by the numbers: plants → grasshoppers → toads → snakes → ducks (each level eats the one below; numbers fall from 1500 to 175 to 60 to 10 above the herbivores).

Textbook (G12 p.110): 'The pyramid of numbers compares the number of individuals at each trophic level … The size of each block in the pyramid represents the numbers of organisms feeding at that level.'

Put the producers (plants, 100) at the base, then grasshoppers (1500), toads (175), snakes (60) and ducks (10) at the top; draw each block with width proportional to the number and label it with organism, number and trophic level.
Because the producers are few but large (Figure 3.14b), the bottom block is narrower than the grasshopper block – a partly inverted (spindle-shaped) pyramid.
marking_points: Correct order of trophic levels with plants (producers) at the base and grasshoppers as primary consumers (1)
Bars drawn roughly proportional to the numbers and labelled with organism/number (1)
Accept either order of snakes and ducks at the top if the student's food chain is explained
tips: Always put producers at the bottom even if they are fewer; label each bar with organism, number and trophic level.

similar_questions.stem: In a field there are 1 tree, 400 caterpillars feeding on it and 20 birds feeding on the caterpillars. Describe the shape of the pyramid of numbers.
similar_questions.answer: Tree 1 (base) → caterpillars 400 → birds 20: the base is very narrow, the middle bar widest and the top narrow – an inverted (spindle-shaped) pyramid of numbers.
explanation_steps: A single large producer supports many small herbivores, so the pyramid of numbers is inverted at the base; a pyramid of biomass would be upright.

questions.review_flag: The paper gives no food chain: the key follows the decreasing numbers (plants → grasshoppers → toads → snakes → ducks), but ducks as predators of snakes is biologically doubtful and some students may put ducks below snakes. The producer bar (100) is smaller than the grasshopper bar (1500), so the correct pyramid is partly inverted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Define the following terms/phrases. 11.1 Coronary circulation 11.2 Vaccines 11.3 Ossification (3 points)
questions.answer: 11.1 Coronary circulation: the circulation of blood within the walls of the heart itself – the coronary arteries (branching from the aorta) supply the heart muscle with oxygen and food, and the coronary veins return the blood to the right atrium. 11.2 Vaccines: antigens (killed or weakened micro-organisms or their products) prepared so that they stimulate the body to make antibodies and memory cells – artificially acquired active immunity – without causing the disease. 11.3 Ossification: the process by which cartilage is gradually converted (replaced) into bone by bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) that deposit calcium salts.

subparts.question: Coronary circulation
subparts.answer: Blood supply of the heart muscle itself through the coronary arteries and veins

subparts.question: Vaccines
subparts.answer: Antigens (weakened/killed germs or their products) that stimulate active immunity without causing disease

subparts.question: Ossification
subparts.answer: Conversion of cartilage into bone (by osteoblasts, deposition of calcium salts)

explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.56): coronary circulation 'supplies blood to the heart muscles. It consists of coronary arteries and coronary veins … The circuit of blood within the walls of the heart itself is called coronary circulation.'
Textbook (G10 p.103): 'Vaccines are antigens prepared in such a way that they promote active immunity without causing the disease.'

Textbook (G11 p.54, 57): 'A bone begins as cartilage before it is converted to bone through a process called ossification'; 'Cartilage is gradually converted to bone by a process called ossification.'
marking_points: 11.1 blood circulation within the heart wall / supplying the heart muscle (1)
11.2 antigens/weakened or dead pathogens that stimulate antibody production (active immunity) without causing the disease (1)
11.3 conversion/replacement of cartilage by bone (bone formation) (1)
tips: Coronary = crown: the coronary arteries encircle the heart like a crown.

similar_questions.stem: Define (a) pulmonary circulation and (b) vaccination.
similar_questions.answer: (a) The circulation of blood from the right ventricle to the lungs (pulmonary arteries) and back to the left atrium (pulmonary veins), where it is oxygenated. (b) The introduction of a vaccine into the body to produce artificial active immunity against a disease.
explanation_steps: Pulmonary = lungs; vaccination gives artificially acquired active immunity.

questions.stem: Draw the structure of a neuron and label the parts given below: axon, dendrite, cell nucleus, cell body, myelin sheath, terminal buttons. (2 points)
questions.answer: A labelled drawing of a (motor) neuron: a rounded cell body (cyton/soma) containing a large cell nucleus; several short branched dendrites projecting from the cell body; one long axon leaving the cell body, wrapped along its length in a segmented myelin sheath (sausage-like beads with gaps – nodes of Ranvier); the axon ends in fine branches carrying small swellings – the terminal buttons (synaptic knobs) – that pass the message to the next cell. Arrow of impulse: dendrites → cell body → axon → terminal buttons.
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.164–166): the cell body (soma) 'contains the nucleus'; dendrites are many branch-like extensions that receive messages; a single long axon carries the impulse away from the cell body.
'Longer axons are usually covered with a myelin sheath, which is a series of fatty cells wrapped around an axon. These make the axon look like a necklace of sausage-shaped beads' (G10 p.165).
The axon ends in terminals (terminal buttons) that release neurotransmitters into the synapse (G10 p.166, 168).
Drawing tips: draw large and clear, use a sharp pencil, label lines ruled and not crossing, all six labels present.
marking_points: Correct outline of a neuron (cell body with dendrites, one long axon ending in branches) (½)
Six correct labels – axon, dendrite, cell nucleus, cell body, myelin sheath, terminal buttons – ¼ point each (1½)
tips: Impulse direction: Dendrite → cell body → Axon → terminals ('DCAT').

similar_questions.stem: State the function of (a) dendrites and (b) the myelin sheath.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Dendrites receive impulses (chemical messages) from other neurons or receptors and carry them towards the cell body. (b) The myelin sheath insulates the axon and speeds up conduction of the nerve impulse.
explanation_steps: G10 p.164–165: myelin works like the insulation round an electric wire.
